Its range is moderate: the top is crisp and nimble, the middle warm and full, the low register steadier and more contained. The resonance of the soundbox produces natural overtones, giving the timbre a drifting, poetic quality. Beside the splendour and weight of the modern harp the Greek harp sounds plainer and more refined; beside the guzheng its timbre has less of deep sorrow and more of freshness and agility. The plucking is varied and flexible and can produce clear single notes or blended harmony; the overall sound is archaic yet expressive, strongly characteristic of Mediterranean civilisation, and often leaves a sense of distant calm.

The lyre is a chordophone of ancient Greece and the Mediterranean world, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.21-5, a yoke lute of the lute family. It is built from a soundbox, two arms and a crossbar, with the strings attached to a yoke in the same plane as the soundboard. In the source it is a plucked instrument, usable with a story or with singing, and the bards of ancient Greece used it to set the mood; some ancient lyres were also played with a plectrum. The Chinese source says its soundbox is comparatively narrow and easy to carry, with mostly five to eight strings, and sometimes fifteen.
